_comment: Claims that circulate about the city, checked against the record this site already publishes. Hand-authored, like data.tax-case.json — nothing here is generated, because deciding what a claim actually asserts is not a thing a script can do. The rules the page states in `how` are binding on this file: a claim is only listed when it can be answered out of an open-meeting recording, a document the city or the state published, or arithmetic on figures from one of those, and every entry carries the citation next to the sentence it supports. Claims are quoted as they circulate and never attributed to a private individual by name; officials speaking in an open meeting are named, because that is the record. `verdict` is one of the keys in `verdicts` below. `checked` is when the entry was last read against the record; a claim about a live dispute goes stale quickly, which is why every card prints that date. `topics` are keys from `categories`, which is what the filter bar at the top of the page is built from: the first topic is the heading a claim files under and the rest are the other shelves it belongs on, because most of these claims are about two things at once.
title: What's going around, and what the record says
sub: Things residents are telling each other about the city — the tax increase, the staffing, the petition — set against the meetings, the notices and the audited figures they can be checked against. Some are true, some are out of date, and the ones the city itself put into circulation get the same treatment as the ones aimed at it.

how.heading: How something gets on this page
rules: It has to be circulating. Not a hypothetical, not a strawman — something being repeated in a comment thread, on a sign, at a hearing, or in the city's own messaging.

It has to be checkable against a source that exists. A recording of an open meeting, a document published by a government body — this city, another one, the county, the state or the federal government — or arithmetic done here on figures from one of those. A claim about how Eagle Mountain compares with anywhere else can only be settled from outside Eagle Mountain, so the sources go where the answer is. If nothing can settle it, the entry says so rather than guessing.
The claim gets quoted; the person doesn't get named. Residents in a comment thread are not public figures. Officials speaking in an open meeting are, and are named.
The city's own claims are checked the same way. Two of the entries below are things the city said, not things said about it.
Every card carries the date it was last checked, because half of these turn on a rate the council has already changed twice.
how.submit: Something being repeated that isn't here? The claim as you heard it, and where you saw it, is enough to start with.

verdicts.label: Accurate

claims.claim: The council raised your property taxes 220 percent.
claims.ruling: 220.88% was noticed in June and never adopted. The rate that survives is 0.000900 — 69.81% over the certified rate, on the city's own line, which is about a twentieth of a property tax bill.
claims.seen: Yard signs, petition sheets and city Facebook groups, June to August 2026
claims.true_part: The number was real and the city printed it. The Truth-in-Taxation notice mailed in June proposed 0.001700 against a 0.000530 certified rate and stated the increase as 220.88% — a rise in the city's budgeted property tax revenue over the prior year, excluding eligible new growth.
claims.wrong_part: Two things. The figure is three rates out of date: the council adopted 0.001500 on August 6, repealed it on August 18, and adopted 0.000900 in its place. And it was never a percentage of anybody's tax bill — it is a percentage of the city's own levy, which is one of seven lines on an Eagle Mountain bill and the fourth-largest of them.
detail: On the notice's own average home — $488,000 of market value, $268,400 taxable after Utah's 55% primary-residence exemption — the noticed rate would have added $314.03 a year. The rate in force adds $99.31.

On that same home the city's line goes from about $143 a year to about $242, inside a total bill of about $2,517 at 2025 rates. That is the city's share moving from roughly 5.7% of the bill to roughly 9.2% of it. Alpine School District's line alone is more than six times the city's.
claims.provisional: The 0.000900 is certain; the vote, the motion and the figures the adopting resolution recites were not published when this was written, so everything priced at that rate here is this project's arithmetic on it.

claims.claim: Every dollar of the increase goes straight to public safety.
claims.claim_note: The city's own claim, not one aimed at it.
claims.ruling: True in the schedule's own terms — the levy is smaller than the Sheriff's contract, so there is no second dollar to allocate. What it left out is that the money largely replaces sales tax already paying that contract, and frees the sales tax for other things.
claims.seen: City messaging, quoted back to the council at the August 6 hearing
claims.true_part: The statutory impact schedule names the Sheriff's contract as the affected budget and puts it at $9,798,139 — the same figure, to the dollar, as the proposed property tax revenue. Designed that way, the levy covers the contract and nothing else.
claims.wrong_part: What actually changes is which pot pays. Property tax takes over a contract sales tax had been subsidising, and the freed sales tax goes to other city spending — parks, roads, staff. That is a defensible policy and it is not what "every dollar goes to public safety" conveys, which is why residents who did the subtraction — $6.74 million noticed against a $1.5 million rise in the contract — concluded they had been lied to.
detail: At the rate finally adopted the gap runs the other way and is larger. 0.000900 raises about $5.19 million against a contract of $9,798,139, so roughly $4.61 million of the Sheriff's contract still comes out of sales tax — four times what the repealed rate would have left short.

claims.claim: They did this in secret and rushed it through.
claims.ruling: Two different charges are tangled together. On whether it was done in the open the record is unusually complete — seven open meetings from April 14, both August hearings set three months ahead, the schedule read into the record four times. On whether residents found out, the council agrees with the criticism: four of five said so from the dais before voting.
claims.seen: Comment threads and hearing testimony, June to August 2026
claims.true_part: Residents did not hear about it in time to weigh in early, and that is not in dispute. The council conceded it on the record before the vote, and the concession is the strongest evidence for the complaint.
claims.wrong_part: Nothing was done outside a noticed public meeting. The Sheriff's Office presented the staffing case in an open work session on April 14; on May 5 the council accepted the tentative budget, acknowledged the proposed increase and declared its intent to exceed the certified rate, setting both August hearings; the impact schedule was read on May 26, June 2 and June 16, and the June 16 hearing ran with public comment answered at length. The August 6 hearing took about sixty speakers over three hours.

claims.claim: The increase pays for the city's own police department.
claims.ruling: Eagle Mountain employs no police officers and no firefighters. Patrol is bought from the Utah County Sheriff's Office; fire and ambulance come from Unified Fire Authority, which bills residents on a separate line of the same tax notice.
claims.seen: Recurring in comment threads whenever the Sheriff's contract comes up
claims.true_part: The money does pay for policing. The affected budget on the impact schedule is the Sheriff's contract, and the deputies it funds are assigned to the Eagle Mountain division.
claims.wrong_part: It is a contract, not a department. The city's audited schedule shows 4.82 full-time equivalents under public safety and every one of them is a crossing guard; the line for firefighters and officers reads zero, and has read zero for eleven years. Fire and ambulance are not the city's at all — Unified Fire Service Area levies 0.001650 directly, which is nearly twice the city's own new rate.
detail: This matters for reading a tax bill. Someone comparing Eagle Mountain's rate against a neighbouring city that runs its own police and fire is comparing a city that buys those services against one that levies for them, and the neighbour's higher rate is partly that difference.

claims.claim: Sign the petition and the tax goes away.
claims.ruling: A referendum on a property tax rate is legally available, and one ran in a Utah city as recently as last autumn. But the resolution a petition was organised against was repealed on August 18 and replaced, and the signature test is two thresholds rather than one.
claims.seen: Petition drives and organising posts, August 2026
claims.true_part: Utah Code § 20A-7-613 exists for exactly this situation. Five sponsors file a notarised application with the resolution attached; the city's budget officer must then produce an unbiased fiscal and legal impact statement within days; then signatures are gathered against a statutory threshold.
claims.wrong_part: Nothing about it is automatic, and two things are genuinely unsettled. The first is what a petition aimed at the August 6 resolution does now that the resolution has been repealed and a smaller increase adopted in its place — that turns on what was filed and when, and the city recorder is the authority on it, not this page. The second is the threshold itself.
detail: For a city of the second class it is 8.25% of active voters citywide and 8.25% within at least 75% of the city's voter participation areas. Both must be met, and the second is what decides these — it is the one almost nobody organising a petition budgets for.

Whether Eagle Mountain is second class yet is itself open. The statutory line is 65,000 residents, the first statewide subcounty estimates put the city at 65,409 in 2025, and the class changes on the lieutenant governor's certificate rather than on the estimate. If that certificate has not issued, the thresholds are 10% rather than 8.25%.

figures.label: Citywide signatures
figures.note: of active voters — 10% if still third class

figures.note: of voter participation areas must each clear 8.25%

claims.claim: They're building another data center in Eagle Mountain.
claims.ruling: Yes, and the votes are on file. What is being built is more of what is already here — every data center approval in the record since 2024 is an expansion by Meta or QTS, not a new company arriving.
claims.seen: A city Facebook group, August 2026; and public comment to the council since at least February 2026
claims.true_part: Three campuses are already named in the city's own record — Meta, Google and QTS — and building has not stopped. QTS's SLC1 site was still under construction this spring, when the council let it work outside the hours city code normally allows. A second QTS parcel, the land the motion calls QTS-SCL 2, was rezoned on March 3. And on October 21 the council approved a development agreement with Stadion, LLC, the company known as Meta, on a 4–1 vote, along with a third amendment to its water and sewer agreement the same night.
claims.wrong_part: “Another” suggests a new operator. Nothing in the record shows one. It is also worth knowing what has not happened yet: the newest land in play — the parcel west of the Pony Express area that QTS has bought — was described to the council on August 4 as still zoned agricultural. Farmland cannot be built on until the council rezones it, and a rezone is a public vote with a public hearing in front of it.
detail: The scale of it gets overstated in both directions. A resident told the council in February that they had read five more had been approved. In the twelve months before that comment the council passed four measures touching the data centers — a road realignment at the Meta site, the Meta development agreement, the water and sewer amendment beside it, and a sign-code rule for directional signage — and none of the four approved a new data center.

The motions themselves are thin, which is a fair complaint about the record rather than about the claim. The QTS-SCL 2 rezone does not state the acreage or the new zoning, and the Meta development agreement does not list its terms. The votes are public; what was voted on is often summarised in a single line.

read_more.label: The claim about the size of it

claims.claim: It's going to be the largest data center in the country, maybe the world.
claims.ruling: No. A single project already approved in Box Elder County covers 40,000 acres — more ground than the whole of Eagle Mountain, which is 32,256 acres of land. Whatever gets built here, the largest in the country is not going in this city.
claims.seen: A city Facebook group, August 2026, in a thread about the new site
claims.true_part: The premise underneath it is sound. Eagle Mountain has three data center campuses, it keeps approving work on them, and QTS has bought more ground west of the Pony Express area that has not been through the council yet. Somebody hearing that a company is buying more land here is hearing something true, and the state as a whole genuinely is getting enormous ones.
claims.wrong_part: It is the superlative that fails, and it fails on a comparison anyone can make. The Stratos project area in western Box Elder County — a data and energy campus approved by the MIDA board on April 24 and agreed to by the Box Elder County Commission on May 4 — covers 40,000 acres. Eagle Mountain City is 50.4 square miles of land, which is 32,256 acres. The project area 200 miles north is about a quarter larger than this entire city, and it is the one Utah newsrooms have been calling the largest in the country.
detail: Two honest qualifications, neither of which rescues the claim. The 40,000 acres is the project area rather than the buildings: the state's own FAQ says most of it will stay undeveloped and the data center footprint will be “a fraction” of it. And those April and May votes created the project area, not the project — the state says plainly that they did not approve the full development, which still needs air, water and wildlife review.

The other half of the problem is local, and it is the more useful half. Nothing Eagle Mountain has voted on states a size for anything. The QTS-SCL 2 rezone does not give the acreage or the zoning it granted; the Meta development agreement does not list its terms. So there is no figure in the city's record that a claim about size could be measured against — which is exactly why a superlative can circulate here for weeks without meeting a number.

claims.claim: The public safety reason was misleading — the tax increase is really to cover up his misdeeds on the rodeo grounds and build their new kingdom.
claims.ruling: There is a new $1 million rodeo-grounds line in the budget, so the question is a fair one to ask. The increase cannot be what pays for it: at the rate in force the whole city levy falls about $4.6 million short of the city's own public safety budget.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.claim_note: “Misdeeds” refers to allegations made in a lawsuit filed against the city in March 2026. The city has formally denied them and no court has ruled on them. The filing and the city's denial are both cited below.
claims.true_part: The budget line is real, and it is new. The FY2026–27 capital schedule carries “Relocate Rodeo Grounds” at $1,000,000 in the Capital Projects General Fund, account 47-81-41000-7078. The year before, the only rodeo line was $80,000 of arena work. A $500,000 City Hall line sits in the same fund. Anyone reading the capital sheet and the tax notice on the same evening would reasonably ask what the money is for.
claims.wrong_part: The increase cannot be the source. Property tax appears in this budget as its own revenue line and, dollar for dollar, as a restricted expense inside Public Safety — the Sheriff contract line was cut to exactly the city's existing property tax collections and the balance moved to that restricted line. At the adopted 0.000900 the whole city levy raises about $5,188,077 against $9,798,139 of budgeted public safety. That is a shortfall of roughly $4.6 million, not a surplus to divert. Capital projects sit in a different fund with different sources.
detail: The capital projects fund is shrinking, not growing: $16,954,637 in FY2026–27 against $19,805,942 the year before, down $2,851,305.
The rodeo relocation is fifteenth on the capital list, below $3,360,000 for a Pony Express trailhead, $2,790,000 for Campus Drive, $2,500,000 for land acquisition and $2,000,000 for Airport Road.

claims.claim: QTS gave 5.5 million dollars to help citizens and the mayor decided to use those funds to fix a road.
claims.ruling: There was no $5.5 million gift. Two figures spoken on the same night have been fused: QTS agreed to pay the roughly $5 million cost of widening Pony Express Parkway, and $5,591,594 was the new revenue from the tax rate the council adopted hours later.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: QTS did commit money, and the mayor did ask for it. On August 6 Mayor Gray told the hearing that the city had been trying to work out how to widen Pony Express Parkway, that he phoned QTS to propose a reimbursement agreement, and that they came back offering to pay the entire bill rather than the half he had asked for.
claims.wrong_part: It was road money in the sentence it was first mentioned — there were never general funds sitting there to be redirected. And the $5.5 million in circulation is a different number from the same meeting: the net revenue above the certified rate that a rate of 0.001500 would raise, $5,591,594, which finance staff computed during the deliberation and which was read into the adopting motion. That rate was repealed twelve days later.
detail: The mayor's stated reason for making the call is the same argument the post makes: that traffic generated by the data center's workers should not be a burden carried by residents.

The wider corridor work is not city property tax either. The $11.4 million Ranches Parkway and Pony Express project discussed on August 4 runs on MAG regional funding, with the city cash-flowing parts of it against a reimbursement interlocal.

claims.claim: Big Tech should have bonded for that road from the beginning.
claims.ruling: A fair criticism with a real fact behind it — the council did cut what commercial builders pay toward roads. It ends with the data center funding the whole project anyway.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: On February 18, 2025 the council voted unanimously — Gray among them — to partially suspend the transportation impact fee for nonresidential development, and removed the restaurant carve-out at every building size. The city chose to charge commercial building less toward roads, and that is the strongest fact available to anyone arguing large employers under-contributed.
claims.wrong_part: The framing assumes a bond was available and refused. Utah cities cannot set a separate tax rate for data centers, and Councilmember Whiting told the August 6 hearing the city already charges the maximum impact fees state law allows. What the city got instead was QTS funding the full cost of the widening, and declining incentives it had already been granted on its next two buildings — more than a bond would have guaranteed on this particular road.

claims.ruling: Both halves hold up against the record. Neither is an allegation on its own, and nothing in the record attaches one to them.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: Gray said from the dais on May 19, 2026, while discussing precast concrete suppliers, that he has “worked in this industry for a long time, and it goes along with excavating gravel pits.” He also argues road geometry with city engineers in more technical detail than anyone else on the dais. On tenure: councilmember 2020–2023 and 2024–2025, mayor since January 1, 2026 — about seven years elected, and eight is fair with prior planning service.
claims.wrong_part: Nothing, as stated. What the claim implies but does not say is a conflict of interest, and the record does not carry one: no city road contract on file is awarded to a business connected to him, and on the item closest to the accusation elsewhere in this post — the rodeo grounds relocation — he did not vote in favour. He abstained.

claims.claim: Why didn't the city make big tech bond for Pony Express since they were going to ruin it from driving on it?
claims.ruling: Put as a failure that already happened. The company is funding the entire project — and a bond is not the instrument that does this job.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The corridor genuinely is the city's biggest cost problem, and residents are right that it has been paid for locally for years. In May 2019 the council approved a UDOT Transportation Infrastructure Fund loan of up to $2,000,000 for widening Pony Express Parkway, and further work ran through 2024 and 2025.
claims.wrong_part: A subdivision improvement bond guarantees that a developer finishes and warranties roads inside its own project, so the city is not left with an unfinished street. There is nothing to guarantee completion of when an existing employer's staff drive an existing public arterial. The lawful tools there are impact fees and negotiated reimbursement or participation agreements — and a reimbursement agreement is what the mayor said he opened the QTS call by proposing. The result was QTS paying the whole bill.

claims.claim: The Waldens built Pony Express 30 years ago. The city has been collecting impact fees for 30 years for that road.
claims.ruling: The founding half is essentially right. The impact fee half describes something Utah law does not permit — a fee has to be spent or committed within six years, not banked for thirty.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The founding is a matter of record. John Walden and two partners bought roughly 8,000 acres in Cedar Valley in 1994; the town of Eagle Mountain incorporated on December 3, 1996 and became a city in 2001. The original parkway came out of that development, and “thirty years” is close enough to right.
claims.wrong_part: Impact fees cannot accumulate that way. Utah's Impact Fees Act requires a city to spend or encumber an impact fee within six years of collecting it, and only on a system improvement named in the impact fee facilities plan for that fee type; holding longer requires a written finding of an extraordinary and compelling reason and a date certain. Nor is it one continuous fee: Eagle Mountain re-enacted its transportation impact fee on May 19, 2020, updated it again on March 6, 2024, and partially suspended it for nonresidential building on February 18, 2025. And for the first two of those thirty years there was no city to collect anything.

sources.speaker: Utah Impact Fees Act
sources.note: A local political subdivision shall expend or encumber an impact fee for a permissible use within six years of collecting it, and may expend impact fees only for a system improvement identified in the impact fee facilities plan for the public facility type the fee was collected for.

sources.note: One of three separate transportation impact fee actions in the record, with an update on 6 March 2024 and a partial suspension on 18 February 2025.

claims.claim: They make builders and developers bond for roads that they could potentially ruin all the time!
claims.ruling: True, and it describes a different instrument doing a different job from the one the post wants it to do.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: Cities do require this constantly, Eagle Mountain included. A subdivision improvement bond is posted as a condition of plat approval and guarantees that the developer builds, completes and warranties the roads inside its own project — so the city is not left holding an unfinished street if the builder walks away. The record carries bond releases as routine consent items.
claims.wrong_part: The posture does not transfer. An operating employer whose staff drive an existing public arterial has no obligation to build to guarantee. The lawful ways to make growth pay for road capacity are impact fees — which the city says it already charges at the statutory maximum — and negotiated reimbursement or participation agreements, which is the route that produced the QTS commitment.

sources.speaker: Councilmember Craig Whiting
sources.note: Said the city charges the maximum impact fees state law allows and cannot tax data centers at a separate rate.

sources.speaker: Utah Impact Fees Act
sources.note: Title 11, Chapter 36a sets out the only mechanism a Utah city has for charging new development toward system improvements, and caps it at the proportionate share the development creates.

claims.claim: Jared should have used 5.5 to build a new jail. Then we would have a revenue source and be able to ticket for city laws and keep all the money from fines instead of giving it to Utah County.
claims.ruling: Right that fine money is going to the county. Wrong about the building that fixes it — that is a justice court, not a jail — and wrong about the scale, which is thousands of dollars, not millions.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The underlying complaint is real, and councilmembers agree with it. Eagle Mountain has no justice court, and its ordinances are not on the county's Master Offense Table, so charges for city-ordinance violations cannot even be filed. A councilmember said on April 14, 2026 that the city had been talking about a justice court “for over 18 months and we're nowhere closer to it.”
claims.wrong_part: Three things. There was no $5.5 million to spend — see the QTS entry. A jail is not the mechanism: what lets a city keep fines from its own ordinances is a justice court, and in Utah the sheriff is the statutory keeper of the county jail, with the nearest booking facility in Spanish Fork. And the money is not there: the entire budgeted general-fund Fines line for FY2026–27 is $6,180, against $9,798,139 of budgeted public safety. A city jail is a cost centre with staffing, medical care and liability attached, not a revenue line.
detail: The city attorney told the council on May 26, 2026 that the city is “legally entitled” to a justice court and that what stands in the way is process, not money for a building.
The broader “Fines & Forfeitures” category in the budget, about $157,700, is mostly NSF fees, library fines, code enforcement fines and late utility charges — not traffic citations.

sources.quote: the discussion came up about getting our city ordinances onto the computer system that allows Utah County Justice Court to actually file charges and for us to actually issue citations for some of these city ordinance violations. You don't have that right now.

sources.speaker: Utah Code on county jails
sources.note: The sheriff shall take charge of and keep the county jail and the prisoners in it. Jails are a county function in Utah; a municipality that wants to keep fines from its own ordinances needs a justice court, which is a court, not a jail.

claims.claim: Brett Wright talked about how broke the city is and how there is NO MONEY.
claims.ruling: Not what the recording has him saying. His argument that night was about choices and about not standing for re-election, not about an empty account.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: Wright did speak at length about the city's finances at the August 6 hearing, and the council as a body did argue that the current revenue mix is not holding. He seconded the motion that set the rate.
claims.wrong_part: What he actually said was that the easy path would have been to do nothing and keep cutting services, and that he is in his fifth year and will not run again — his stated reason for voting without an electoral calculation in it. The council's case was structural rather than “no money”: sales tax is being consumed by the sheriff's contract, leaving intersections without signals; sales tax collapses in a downturn and the need for police does not; and Councilmember Wood put the city's share of the master transportation plan at $419 million by 2035. Residents in the same room argued the opposite — that the city already has the money.
detail: The transcript of this meeting is now speaker-attributed, so the remarks above can be read against his name rather than inferred. The chair hands off to each member by name before they speak — “Okay, thank you. Councilmember Wright, go ahead” — and Wright's reply runs from there to “My time's about out, but thank you for being here.” Nothing in it says the city has no money.

The later open deliberation is a different matter: after about 03:42 members interrupt each other and the chair stops introducing anyone, so that stretch is left unattributed on the site rather than guessed. The second quotation below sits in that stretch, which is why it is credited to a councilmember and not to a named one.

sources.quote: We have intersections that are missing traffic control signals because we can't afford to put them in. Where does that money come from? If we continue to pull sales tax dollars, which could fund those infrastructure improvements, and we continue to allocate it to our sheriff's contract…

claims.claim: Build a revenue source. Like owning your own utilities or owning your own police officers.
claims.ruling: The city already owns its utilities, on a scale six times its general fund. And city-owned police is exactly what the tax increase funds — the same policy this post's opening sentence calls a cover story.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: Both are sound instincts about municipal finance, and the second one is city policy. Eagle Mountain employs no police officers today: patrol is bought from the Utah County Sheriff's Office, and fire and ambulance come from Unified Fire Authority, which bills residents on a separate line of the same tax notice.
claims.wrong_part: The utilities half describes something that has been true for years. Eagle Mountain runs water, sewer, storm drain and solid waste as city-owned funds, plus an internal utility billing fund; in FY2026–27 those total roughly $269.7 million against a $42.7 million general fund, and on February 17, 2026 the council authorised up to $220,000,000 in water and sewer revenue bonds. The police half is the increase itself. A post cannot call public safety a pretext in its first line and propose city-owned police as the alternative in its ninth.
detail: Municipal utilities in Utah are also rate-funded enterprises, not general revenue: an enterprise fund charges users for the service and is expected to cover its own costs, which is why a water fund cannot quietly subsidise a police department.

claims.claim: And Jared has been out asking everyone he can for new RODEO GROUNDS, I heard.
claims.ruling: Relocating the rodeo grounds is real, funded and entirely on the public record. It is also a council decision the mayor declined to vote for.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The substance is right. On April 15, 2025 the council adopted a resolution expressing intent to work with the West Traverse Sentinel Landscape committee on relocating the rodeo grounds into the Army Compatible Use Buffer around Camp Williams, and the FY2026–27 capital schedule carries $1,000,000 for it.
claims.wrong_part: The framing, and the sourcing. This is not a quiet errand by one man: it is a noticed agenda item that passed 4–0, with Wright, Burnham, Clark and Wood in favour — and Jared Gray abstaining. He is the one person on that dais who did not vote for it. The sourcing offered for the quiet part is “I heard.”
detail: The line sits fifteenth on the FY2026–27 capital list, below $3,360,000 for a Pony Express trailhead, $2,790,000 for Campus Drive, $2,500,000 for land acquisition and $2,000,000 for Airport Road. The capital projects fund as a whole is down $2,851,305 year over year.

claims.claim: I offered to fix the eagle by 73 for free since it was ours and was never called back. The city could have saved money.
claims.ruling: A private offer and an unreturned phone call leave no trace in an open-meeting record, so this site cannot settle it either way. What can be checked is what happened to the monument.
claims.seen: Eagle Mountain City Tax Referendum Facebook group, August 2026
claims.true_part: The eagle monument was down, it mattered to people, and the city spent money putting it back. A councilmember said on May 19, 2026 that residents cared about it more than anyone realised — “until it was gone.”
claims.wrong_part: Nothing is contradicted, and nothing is confirmed. Offers made by phone do not appear in agendas, minutes or recordings, which are the only things this page checks claims against. It would be settled by a written offer or by the city's correspondence — a records request, not a meeting recording.
detail: What the record does carry: by April 28, 2026 city staff had rebuilt the retaining wall and the contractor had poured the footings and pad, with installation scheduled for around the end of May. It was named as one of the few capital projects expected to finish without rolling into the next year.
